During our hardware in the loop tests, we hit a severe priority inversion inside the FreeRTOS kernel. The low priority logging task at priority 3 held the shared telemetry ring buffer while the medium priority motor control task consumed 80 percent of the CPU time. Because the logging task could not run, the high priority safety monitor task stalled for 50 milliseconds waiting for the resource.

We traced this lockup to our choice of synchronization primitive, where the firmware used a binary semaphore instead of a mutex. Binary semaphores do not support priority inheritance, so the low priority worker never inherited the high priority level of the waiting safety task.

Write the fix by replacing the binary semaphore with a FreeRTOS mutex with priority inheritance enabled. This allows the low priority task to finish flushing and release the lock immediately.

On the Cortex-M7 platform, we observed data corruption during high speed SPI sensor capture using DMA. The DMA controller writes incoming packets directly to SRAM starting at 0x20004000, but when the CPU reads the packet buffer, it receives stale sensor values from the internal L1 data cache because the cache controller does not know the memory changed.

To resolve this cache coherency issue, we must invalidate the D-cache lines covering the destination buffer before the CPU inspects the payload. Similarly, whenever the firmware prepares an outgoing transmission buffer, the CPU must clean the cache, write the dirty lines back to physical SRAM before triggering the DMA channel.

Otherwise the DMA engine reads old values from memory. We can also configure an MPU region as non-cacheable for shared descriptor rings.

Our power audit revealed that several unused GPIO pins remained configured as floating inputs rather than analog mode. Switching off the internal buffer and gating the RTC wakeup timer for a 60 second interval reduced total sleep current to 12 microamps. Calibrating the RTC prescaler ensures accurate periodic wakeups without waking the CPU early.

Migrating from legacy I2C to the modern I3C protocol introduces dynamic address assignment during bus initialization. The main master controller broadcasts the enter dynamic address assignment command across the shared bus. Each secondary target node pulls the serial data line low using open-drain signaling during address arbitration.

The device with the lowest provisional identifier wins the arbitration slot by asserting its vendor and part identification bits. Once the controller assigns a 7 bit dynamic address, the target acknowledges and releases the bus, allowing the next peripheral to participate.

After all secondary targets receive unique addresses, the bus transitions from open-drain mode to push-pull mode for high speed data transfers up to 12 megahertz.

The bus exhibited ringing voltages exceeding 2 volts during dominant bit transitions, which caused receivers to miss the sample point and trigger form errors. Our inspection showed that the far end node lacked a 120 ohm termination resistor.

By installing the missing resistor and shortening the stub wiring from 40 centimeters down to 5 centimeters, we eliminated reflections and restored a clean differential voltage swing.

We also adjusted the nominal bit timing prescaler so the sample point shifted to 80 percent of the bit duration. This timing alignment allows the transceivers to reliably decode packet data across 20 consecutive transmission cycles.

When we sampled high impedance thermistors with short sample times of 3 cycles, the measured voltages suffered from channel cross talk and inaccurate temperature readings.

To resolve this issue, we increased the sampling time to 48 cycles for all thermistor channels and enabled the internal buffer amplifier.

We also read the factory calibration bandgap reference voltage at address 0x1fff75a0. By comparing the measured bandgap value with the factory constant, the firmware dynamically compensates for power supply voltage drift.
